title: A guest at the Friday table
hookLine: invited to a Friday-night dinner for the first time: what happens, and what nobody expects of you
carry: you don't have to know the words

cards: The text says: come for Shabbat dinner, Friday, seven. Maybe it's your partner's parents. Maybe a coworker, a college Hillel, a friend who just started hosting.
Maybe you're Jewish and have never actually been to one. And the questions start. What do I bring?
Do I need to know Hebrew? What if everyone stands up and I'm still sitting? A Friday table is built for guests.
Inviting people, especially people with nowhere else to go, is one of the oldest parts of Shabbat. Today: what to expect when you're the one walking in.

teach.b: Start at the door. The greeting is Shabbat shalom, a peaceful Sabbath. In some homes you'll hear the Yiddish, gut Shabbos.

Come on time, or a little early, because in many homes the candles are lit before sunset, and in observant homes the host won't drive, cook, or answer the phone once Shabbat begins. Flowers are a safe gift.
If you'd like to bring food or wine, ask first, since many hosts keep kosher. Then the evening has an order, and most of it is joyful. A song, often Shalom Aleichem.

In many homes, parents bless their children. Then Kiddush, the blessing over a cup of wine or grape juice; some families stand for it, some sit, and you just do what the table does. Then the part that surprises guests.

Many people get up and wash their hands at a sink, pouring water from a cup, and then go quiet. Nobody's upset. There's a custom of not talking between washing and the blessing over the bread, so the two stay joined.
Then the challah is blessed, often sprinkled with salt, torn and passed around. And then dinner, which can go on for hours.
What nobody expects of you: to know the Hebrew, to sing along, or to pretend to be anything you're not. Listening is enough. Asking is better.
What's this for? is a question most hosts are delighted to answer. The rabbis even taught that welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence. You're not intruding on the evening.
You're part of what it's for.

how: Many Jewish families and communities invite guests for Friday-night dinner, including friends, partners and people who would otherwise be alone; guests are welcome to follow along, ask questions and join in as much or as little as they like.

games.q: you're a guest. everyone washes their hands and suddenly nobody's talking. what do you do?
o: stay quiet and follow along until the bread is blessed.
games.why: many families keep quiet between washing the hands and the blessing over bread, so the two stay joined. the talking comes right back with the challah.

practice: Picture a Friday evening door opening on burning candles, and your Shabbat shalom. Picture a seat, a cup, a piece of torn bread, and let any nervousness soften; nobody at this table is grading you.
If you're usually the host, picture welcoming one person who'd be alone on a Friday night.

wordCard.voice: Shabbat shalom. A peaceful Sabbath: the greeting at the door on Friday night, for hosts and guests alike.

carryVoice: Your line: you don't have to know the words. A guest who shows up and asks good questions is doing it right. Day one hundred one.
